own_scenes.desc: Savage dejó fuera el ska por la casi imposibilidad de fechar los discos, pero estaba en todas partes: Peter Meaden veía en 1964 un movimiento mod que solo tenía pop americano, R&B y «una pizca de ska jamaicano»; Island editó desde 1963 una avalancha de ska y Chris Blackwell diversificó con Sue; en Le Duce y en Tiles sonaban Prince Buster, Desmond Dekker o los Wailers, y en Tiles el ska llegó a dominar: «cualquiera podía bailar un disco de ska», y por primera vez la juventud negra se mezclaba en los clubes. La discografía del libro recoge algunos sencillos del año.

refs.q: Moving like you were from the West Indies. Practically anybody could dance to a ska record.
refs.para: ‘All the dances were kind of thrown into one. The latecomer mods were doing what they called the Block, which was used in other Soho nightclubs. And, of course, from ’63 there had been a lot of influence from ska and blue beat. Moving like you were from the West Indies. Practically anybody could dance to a ska record. Ska at Tiles became dominant, in a way. A lot of the younger boys came from the working class; it was the first time we were getting a good crossover of black youth in the clubs as well.’

podcast.title: First Wave (1962-Late 1960s)
podcast.body: The "first wave" of Ska began in 1962 when Cecil Bustamenta Campbell and guitarist Jerry Jha shifted the beat emphasis from the one and three to the two and four, stressing the offbeat. This coincided with Jamaica's independence from Britain, making Ska the semi-official sound of the Independence Movement. The Skatalites were a key studio band during this era. "The big change happened in 1962 when one of Coxen's buddies, Cecil Bustamenta Campbell, changed the beat. Cecil and his guitarist Jerry Jha moved the beat emphasis from the one and the three to the two and the four. So in other words, they began to stress the offbeat. And this is pretty much when Scott was born."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: National Music of Independent Jamaica (1962)
podcast.body: Upon Jamaica's independence in 1962, Ska music, being homegrown and representing a "good time music" vibe, became a significant cultural symbol for the new nation. "In 1962, Jamaica became an independent nation, and this new SCOP music was exactly what the country needed. It was good time music, and it was homegrown."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Spread to Britain and Beyond (1964)
podcast.body: Jamaican immigrants brought Ska to Britain, where a diaspora was serviced by at least three record labels by 1964. The music was then discovered by white British youth, especially mods, and further popularized by Millie Small's worldwide hit "My Boy Lollipop." "By 1964, the Jamaican diaspora in Britain was being serviced by at least three record labels that brought music from home. Eventually, it was discovered by white kids, especially those identifying as mods, and spread the sounds even further."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ska Became Jamaica's National Dance – Skanking; Then Reggae Took Over by 1969
podcast.body: Ska was the dominant music of Jamaica through the mid-1960s and was essentially the national dance of the new country. The dance was called skanking — bend the knees, run in place, make fists, bend the elbows, punch and step to the beat. By the late 1960s, poverty and political unrest in Kingston and Montego Bay's ghettos produced the Rude Boys — alienated, unemployed youth who ran dances with big sound systems. The music slowed down and became more menacing, becoming reggae. This ended the first wave of ska by 1969. "SCA became the semi-official sound of this new country."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Not-So Brief History of Ska: Part 1

podcast.title: Don Letts DJ'd Reggae at the Roxy (1976–77) – Punk Fans Embraced the Anti-Establishment Bass Lines and "Musical Reportage"
podcast.body: Don Letts, later an associate of the Clash and a member of Big Audio Dynamite, was DJing only reggae at the Roxy club in 1976–77 to punk audiences. The punk crowd connected with reggae's "musical reportage quality" — the fact that songs were about something — the obvious anti-establishment stance, the bass lines, and the weed. This cross-pollination of punk and ska created the second wave. "Like minded spirits, you know, they were kind of reveled certainly on the streets of London that were thrown together as outsiders."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Not-So Brief History of Ska: Part 1

podcast.title: Third Wave's California Roots – Bay Area Uptones (1981) Inspired Hardcore + Ska Fusion; Secret Sauce for Third Wave
podcast.body: The third wave began in the Bay Area with The Uptones (1981), a group of 15 and 16-year-olds fascinated by the Two-Tone sound. They played tons of Bay Area shows for seven years, inspiring other groups. The next generation added hardcore punk DNA to the mix — this was the secret sauce that set the stage for the third wave. Fishbone (formed 1979) also kept ska alive through the mid-1980s in California, mixing punk, funk, soul, metal, and ska with social commentary about racism, oppression, and nuclear war. "Hardcore punk rock. And this was the secret sauce that set things up for what would be the third wave of Scott."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Not-So Brief History of Ska: Part 2

podcast.title: Second Wave (Late 1970s-1985)
podcast.body: The "second wave" of Ska emerged in the UK in the wake of punk, fueled by Jamaican immigrants who moved to Britain after Jamaica's independence due to a post-war labor shortage. It was initially known as "Bluebeat" and coexisted with R&B, Soul, and Reggae, embraced by British youth subcultures like mods, rockers, teddy boys, and early punks. "The second wave came in the wake of punk. Jamaica became an independent nation in 1962, so no more British colony."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Ska's US Midwest – Gangster Fun (Detroit, 1986); Mustard Plug; Skapone
podcast.body: While the Toasters (New York) and Bosstones (Boston) established ska on the coasts, the Midwest was served by Detroit's Gangster Fun (formed 1986), who spread the Two-Tone sound in the same DIY spirit — their 1989 debut was released only in the UK. Other Midwest ska bands included Mustard Plug and Skapone. "Since no one knew about Skah, they decided to spread the word themselves."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: A Not-So Brief History of Ska: Part 2

podcast.title: Fourth Wave (2002-Present)
podcast.body: The "fourth wave" began to emerge between 2002 and 2004, driven by a new generation of Ska bands and the continued activity of second and third-wave groups (e.g., The Specials reuniting, Rancid and Reel Big Fish finding new fans, Fishbone still active). This wave respects Ska traditions but introduces new elements, sometimes called "progressive Ska." "Now for there to be a 4th wave, we had to have cooperation from both 2nd and 3rd wave bands. The specials that Key Band from the 2nd wave got back together 40 years after they last recorded together."

podcast.title: Definition and Structure
podcast.body: Ska is defined as a choppy form of music in 4/4 time, characterized by an emphasis on the second and fourth beat of each bar, augmented by the guitar hitting on the first and third, and sometimes fourth beat. The guitar technique used is called the "Ska upstroke," contributing to its very danceable quality. The bass line typically plays steady quarter notes up and down the scale. Brass instruments like trombone or saxophone are often included for added effect. "SCA is a choppy form of music in 4x4 time. The key is the timing of the emphasis on the beat. It's on the second and fourth beat of each bar. That's augmented by the guitar, hitting on the first and third, and sometimes on the fourth beat."

podcast.title: Emergence in Jamaica (Late 1950s)
podcast.body: Ska, initially nicknamed "SCOP," developed in Jamaica from late 1959. It originated from a mix of calypso, soul music, American blues, and R&B, fostered by sound system culture in Kingston's expanding ghettos. This cultural shift was a social effect of wide-scale bauxite mining in Jamaica, which displaced thousands and led to high unemployment. "Starting at about late 1959, this mix of music began to coalesce into something with a distinctive Jamaican sound. Long story short, it was nicknamed SCOP."

"For two years, SCOP was one of the biggest sounds in the UK, but it burned out in the early 1980s. podcast.title: Four Waves of Evolution and Persistence
podcast.body: Ska, born in Jamaica in the 1950s, is a genre that "never, ever goes away," constantly ebbing, flowing, mutating, and evolving. It has seen four distinct waves: the first from Jamaica (Desmond Dekker, Toots and the Maytals, The Skatalites), the second from England in the late 70s/early 80s (cross-bred with punk), the third in the 1990s (No Doubt, Mighty Mighty Bosstones, Sublime), and the fourth arriving in the late 2010s, extending into the new decade, with bands like Captain Ska, The Steady 45s, Los Aggrotones, and The Interrupters. "There have been four distinct waves of Scott since the style was born in Jamaica in the 1950s." "The fourth wave arrived late in the 2010s and bled over into the new decade."

podcast.title: Jamaican Independence and Bauxite Mining – Why Jamaicans Moved to UK; Why Ska Arrived in Britain
podcast.body: Jamaica's desire and ability to stop being a British colony was aided by foreign investment in bauxite mining (Jamaica became the world's number one bauxite producer by 1957 thanks to investor Sir Alfred DeCosta). Young people sold or were removed from rural land by the bauxite miners and moved to cities, settling in ghettos like Trench Town. Starting in 1948, Britain offered all colonials the right to live in the UK due to a post-war labor shortage, and many Jamaicans emigrated to UK cities like Brixton and Coventry, bringing ska (locally called "Bluebeat") with them. In Coventry, bluebeat existed alongside Northern Soul, R&B, reggae, and the mod youth movement — mods were huge fans of all these sounds. "Starting in 1948, Britain said, hey, all you colonials, you have the right to live with us."

podcast.title: Origins of Ska – Jamaica 1950s; African Rhythms + Jazz/R&B + Calypso + Mento = Shuffle, Then Ska
podcast.body: Ska was born in Jamaica in the years following World War II. Big Band, Dixieland, Jazz, Blues, and R&B were heard over shortwave radio from places like New Orleans and from American military personnel in the Caribbean. These were mixed with Caribbean rhythms including Calypso (from Trinidad and Tobago, descended from Biguine, a form of French music co-opted by African slaves) and Mento (Jamaican folk music based on traditional sounds from Africa). This musical stew became known as Shuffle and was heard on Jamaican national radio through the late 1950s and early 1960s. In 1962, Cecil Bustamante Campbell (Prince Buster) changed the beat emphasis to the 2 and 4, and ska was born. "So we have Dixieland, we have Jazz, Blues, R&B, Calypso and Minto. This musical stew became known as Schuffle."

podcast.title: Third Wave Flavors and Global Reach
podcast.body: Third wave Ska, also known as "Ska Punk," had several distinct flavors, with some bands leaning more punk/metal (like Rancid) and others exploring new wave sounds (like No Doubt). While California was the epicenter, third wave Ska became a global phenomenon with scenes in Canada, Spain, Germany, Japan, Argentina, and Russia. It began to melt away by the early 2000s but remains popular. "SCAT Punk, as it became known, had several flavors. Take this group out of Orange County, who struggled through two albums, before something really got weird, with a 1995 album called Tragedy Kingdom."

podcast.title: Third Wave Influences
podcast.body: American punk underground fans, enchanted by the British Ska revival, fused Ska with hardcore influences for the third wave. Early examples include The Mighty Mighty Bosstones from Boston, and later Rancid. Other bands included Voodoo Glow Skulls, Reel Big Fish, Less Than Jake, Buck-O-Nine, and Dance Hall Crashers. "Given their background they inevitably fused SCAT with hardcore influences. So we're going to start on the East Coast in Boston with the Mighty Mighty Boss Tones."

podcast.title: Third Wave Ska (1990s US)
podcast.body: The "third wave" of ska originated in the United States in the 1990s. This iteration took the foundational beats and rhythms of the first and second waves and infused them with elements of angsty punk rock. "Third wave Skop is rooted in the US, starting in the 1990s. It takes the original beats and rhythms of first and second wave Skop and adds some angsty punk rock."

podcast.title: Third Wave Ska – California Radio Show "The Ska Parade" and CD Compilations Created Critical Mass
podcast.body: Third wave ska gathered strength on both the East and West Coasts of the US in the late 1980s and early 1990s. Key to its spread in California was a radio show called The Ska Parade, which played classics alongside newer material by bands like Rancid, Skankin' Pickle, Real Big Fish, Let's Go Bowling, Buckle 9, and Goldfinger. CD compilations from the show further cemented ska into the alternative rock psyche of California, especially in Orange County and south of Los Angeles. "The ska became deeply entrenched into the new music psyche of California, especially in Orange County and to the area south of Los Angeles."

podcast.title: UK Ska Fashion Descent
podcast.body: The clothing styles adopted by the UK Ska scene were directly descended from the original Ska clothes worn in Jamaica. This tradition emphasized sharp, fitted suits in dark colors such as black, navy blue, and chocolate, maintaining a formal yet distinct look. "The clothes for UK SCA descended from the SCA clothes of Jamaica. Sharp suits and dark colors like black, navy blue and chocolate were required."

podcast.title: Versatility and Danceability
podcast.body: The genre's choppy beat was compared to punk, but it could express both anger and happiness, making it highly suitable for dancing. "It could be made angry or happy and it was just great for dancing."

podcast.title: Why "Ska"? – Murky Origin: Guitar Sound, Clue J. Johnson's Made-Up Word, Byron Lee, or The Skatalites
podcast.body: The origin of the word "ska" is murky. Theories include: it was taken from the sound of the choppy guitar click (ska-ska-ska); a Jamaican musician named Clue J. Johnson liked to say "ska-vuvie" all the time; Byron Lee, leader of a band called the Dragonaires, coined it; or The Skatalites invented it when they changed their name from The Satellites. "The origins of the word SCA are a little murky."
